NOTES: According to the notebook, the coin was “found on top of North Central Pier [of the Northeast Gate] looking as if it had been there all along ….”  Actually, the coin must have reached its find-spot subsequent to 1909, since a photograph made in that year by William Bell Dinsmoor Sr. shows some five courses of masonry preserved above the present topmost course.

With a pine tree behind the canopy this coin seems to be a unique variety.  No. xxx is wrongly attributed to Caracalla in Isthmia II, p. 110, note 14. Num. Or. Latin, p. 313, no. 1C, pl. XII, 10; Corinth 6, p. 152, no. 4; Agora 2, p. 76, no. 1935; Corinth 3.1, p. 66-67, argues that the series with “Corinti” was issued by Guilaume de Villerhardouin and that with “Corintum” by Geoffrey II de Villehardouin (1218-1245).  The line of evidence he adduced, the relative number of the types preserved, is now clearer.  Thus, Corinth 6 reported 137 for “Corinti” and Castle Gate, 194 for “Corintum” and Acrocorinth; and Agora 2, reported 49 for the former and 276 for the latter.  The total for these two sites are “Cortini” 186 and “Corintum” 470, strengthening the conclusion that the latter were struck by Geoffrey (1218-45) and the former by William (1245-50), before the establishment of the mint at Clarenza.  The “Genoese” gate thus becomes  a gate of Acrocorinth, as Bellinger argued in Corinth 3.2.
